doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

chapter: Dixieland and the college jazz scene
title: The Dixieland revival and the commercial swing bands
summary: Asked about jazz at Hamilton, he explains Dixieland revival, its West Coast and Condon camps, and why serious fans called swing commercial.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Fascinating. Tell me about playing jazz at Hamilton.

Well yeah, now there’s a lot to be said about all of that. If you read the jazz history books you do not understand that what was called Dixieland jazz, what we probably call classic jazz or trad jazz or something of that kind, was the most popular form of jazz in the United States. You had, beginning in around 1936, you began to have the so-called Dixieland revival. And I won’t go into all the detail of that because it’d take too long. But you began having these bands, people as a result of the swing boom there was a sense that the public was ready for a hotter kind of music. There had been a hot music in the 1920s, then came the depression and hot music was in trouble, now the hot music is back again. And a lot of the players said hey we can maybe, we don’t have to sit in the swing bands, maybe we can go out and play the kind of music we originally came into music to play. And so you began having these bands — on the west coast you had Lu Watters and so forth and those bands playing real, going back to Oliver and going back to Armstrong Hot Fives and so forth. In the sound you had people digging up Bunk Johnson and those

guys and bringing them out. And around the northeast it was more the Condon group with the Wild Bill Davison with George Brunies, Pee Wee Russell and Hall, Bobby Hackett, Teagarden, you know, those names. And so by the late thirties, early forties, if you were interested in jazz it was this, it was Dixieland jazz, or whatever term you want to use. And you began to score in the swing bands. Now Benny Goodman, aww come on, that’s swing. It was these Condon bands or the Lu Watters band or Bunk Johnson or whatever it was, Sidney Bechet had had this big revival. Whatever it was, that was it. And this was what the dyed in the wool, the serious jazz fan, was listening to. Not the dance bands. Not the Harry James. Not anything like that. It was this.
Was that considered, did they use the word “commercial”?

Oh yeah it was commercial. This is commercial crap. And a lot of the baby got thrown out with the bath water a good deal of the time. But you have to remember if you listen to the best of Benny Goodman or the best of Count Basie or the best of Duke Ellington, whatever, you hear a lot of wonderful stuff. If you listen to a complete, the complete Bunny Berigan for example, you hear one dreary dance tune after the next. One after the next. One after the next, with a vocal and so forth and so on. So that the percentage of really good jazz that was being played by those bands was, in some cases, maybe fifty percent. Maybe in the case of say a Goodman or Basie, it might be half. But in the case of a lot of these bands it was a quarter or a third or none. So that a lot of standard swing band stuff was really not of appeal to jazz fans. So that was commercial. Over here was the pure stuff. And right at the same time, because of a lot of factors partly having to do with the war and to the strike, Putrillo’s strike of the musician’s union, there were a lot of reissue programs going out. So now you could go down to a store and buy an album which was an album with four or five or three records in it.
